Vladimir Lenin. The revolutionary leader who founded the Soviet Union and the first communist state in the world, from eighteen seventy to nineteen twenty-four. Born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov in rural Russia, he adopted the pseudonym Lenin as a revolutionary. His elder brother was hanged for plotting against the Tsar, an event that radicalized young Vladimir and pushed him toward revolutionary politics.

After moving through illegal agitation and multiple exiles, he returned to Russia in April nineteen seventeen during the chaos of World War I. He published The State and Revolution, a foundational text arguing that the working class could not use existing capitalist states but must destroy and replace them entirely. He led the Bolsheviks, the revolutionary faction of Russian Marxists, in the October Revolution in nineteen seventeen that toppled the liberal provisional government.

Lenin consolidated Bolshevik power through the Russian Civil War from nineteen eighteen to nineteen twenty-two against anti-communist White forces backed by Western powers and intervening Allied armies. He established democratic centralism as the organizational principle: absolute obedience to central party leadership once decisions were made, silencing dissent within the party.

During the civil war he implemented war communism, seizing grain and resources, and later introduced the New Economic Policy in the nineteen twenties to stabilize the economy. From nineteen twenty-two onward he suffered a series of strokes that marked his final years with illness and concern about succession as he grew increasingly wary of Stalin.

He died in nineteen twenty-four, leaving his successor Stalin to transform the Soviet state into a totalitarian superpower, reversing some of Lenin's more moderate policies. His ideas connect to the Soviet Union he founded, the theoretical framework of Marxism that he adapted and applied, the Russian Revolution he orchestrated, and his rival Trotsky who lost the succession struggle to Stalin.
